1.open: Have you ever been the new person somewhere, like a new job, school or town? What helped you feel like you belonged?
questions: Verses 3 and 4 describe young men who were "gifted in all wisdom" and chosen for the king's palace. What do you think it was like to be talented and valued by the same empire that had just conquered your home?
Verse 7 says the chief official "gave them new names." Names matter. What do you think was lost, and what might they have held onto, when their names were changed?
Verse 8 says Daniel "made up his mind that he would not defile himself." Where in your own life have you had to decide ahead of time what you would or would not go along with?
Daniel asked "for permission" (v. 8) and offered a ten day test (v. 12) instead of making a scene. What do you notice about how he handled the situation, and when is that approach hard to practice?
Verse 9 says "God had granted Daniel favor and compassion from the chief official." Where do you see God at work through other people, even people outside the faith, in this chapter?

The text does not say exactly why the royal food was a problem, and readers differ on whether it was food laws, idols or depending on the king. How does not knowing the reason change how you read Daniel's choice?
Verse 17 says "God gave knowledge and understanding" to the four young men. How does it change the story that their success is credited to God and not to their own effort?

Daniel lived far from home in a culture that did not share his faith. What would help you stay loyal to God in a place like that, and what makes it hard? Feel free to answer honestly if you are not sure what you believe.
1.life: Think of one place this week where you are expected to fit in, such as work, school or a social group. Decide ahead of time one small thing you will quietly hold on to, and one thing you can go along with in good conscience.
1.prayer: Thank God that he is present with people far from home. Ask for wisdom to know what to hold on to and what to let go of, and for kindness toward people who see things differently.
1.tip: The chapter never says why Daniel refused the food, and people will want to settle it. Say plainly that readers differ, then steer the group back to what is clear: Daniel was respectful, thoughtful and firm, and the writer says God was at work.

2.open: Have you ever had a dream so strange or vivid that you could not stop thinking about it the next day?
questions: The king cannot sleep because his spirit is "anxious to understand" his dream (v. 3). What tends to keep you awake at night, and what do you do with it?
The advisers say, "No one on earth can do what the king requests!" (v. 10). Why do you think a powerful man like Nebuchadnezzar reacted with such fury when his advisers admitted their limits?
Daniel "responded with discretion and tact" when the guards came to kill him (v. 14). What does it look like to stay calm and respectful when someone with power over you is being unreasonable?
Daniel did not pray alone. He urged his friends "to plead for mercy from the God of heaven" (v. 18). Who do you turn to when you are afraid, and what makes it hard to ask for help in prayer?

In his song, Daniel says God "changes the times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes them" (v. 21). How does it feel to hear that God is above every leader and government? Does it comfort you, challenge you, or leave you with questions?
Daniel says the secret was revealed "not because I have more wisdom than any man alive" (v. 30). Why might he say that to a king, and how do you handle credit when something goes well for you?

The dream ends with a kingdom God sets up that "will never be destroyed" (v. 44), though Christians differ on how and when that kingdom comes. Whatever your view, what do you hope that kingdom will be like? If you are unsure about it, what questions would you want to ask?
The king says, "Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings" (v. 47). What do you think it takes for someone to move from being impressed by God to actually trusting him?
2.life: Daniel took a frightening problem to his friends and prayed with them. This week, pick one worry and ask a trusted friend or family member to pray about it with you, in person or by phone.
2.prayer: Praise God as the one who "reveals the deep and hidden things" (v. 22). Ask him for calm in the things that worry you, and trust for the things you cannot control.
2.tip: People will want to spend the whole time matching the four metals to specific empires. Say plainly that Christians disagree on this, then steer back to the main point: God is in charge of every kingdom, and his kingdom lasts. Invite quieter members to share what the chapter says to them, not just what it predicts.

3.open: Have you ever gone along with a crowd when you didn't really want to? What happened?
questions: The herald says that when the music plays, "you must fall down and worship the golden statue" (v. 5). What are the cues and pressures today that tell people what to bow to, like success, image or fitting in?
Some astrologers "maliciously accused the Jews" (v. 8). Why might someone report these three? What does that show about the cost of standing out?
The king asks, "Then what god will be able to deliver you from my hands?" (v. 15). Where do you hear a question like that today, a voice saying God can't or won't help?
The three say God is able to save them, and then add, "But even if He does not" (v. 18). How is that different from trusting God only when he rescues?
Have you ever prayed for rescue and it did not come? You can be honest here, including if it left you with doubts. What was that like?

The king sees "four men, unbound and unharmed" in the fire (v. 25). Christians differ on whether the fourth was an angel or Christ. Whichever you think, what does it say that someone was with them in the fire?

The king says the three "risked their lives rather than serve or worship any god except their own God" (v. 28). What did he and the watching officials learn from seeing them? What does their example ask of us?
3.life: Write down one thing you would refuse to do, even if refusing cost you and no rescue came. Then notice one small place this week where you quietly go along with something you don't believe in, and decide one kind, calm way to stand differently.
3.prayer: Ask God for the kind of loyalty the three men showed, trust that does not depend on how things turn out. Pray for anyone in the group who feels like they are in a fire right now.
3.tip: Verses 17 and 18 can sting for anyone who prayed for rescue and did not get it. Don't turn the story into a promise that God always saves, or a claim that faith means being fine. Let people say what is hard, and point to the fourth figure: God was with them in the fire, not only after it.

4.open: Think of a time you were sure you had something all figured out, and life showed you otherwise. What happened?
questions: The chapter opens as the king's own letter to his whole empire, and he begins by praising God: "How great are His signs, how mighty His wonders!" (v. 3). Why might someone choose to tell an embarrassing story about themselves in public? What does it take to do that?
The king says he was "at ease in my house and flourishing in my palace" when the dream came (v. 4). Why do you think warnings so often arrive when life feels comfortable?
The tree in the dream gave food and shelter to every creature (v. 12). What was good about the king's power? What could go wrong when one person holds that much?

The dream's purpose is stated in verse 17: "so that the living will know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind." How do you react to the idea that God is in charge of who holds power? What questions does it raise for you?
Daniel is "perplexed" and alarmed before he speaks (v. 19). Have you ever had to tell someone a hard truth? What made it difficult, and what do you notice about how Daniel handles it?

Daniel urges the king to "Break away from your sins by doing what is right, and from your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed" (v. 27). Why do you think Daniel connects humility with how we treat people who have less power?

The king boasts, "Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built" (v. 30). Where do you see that same voice in our culture, or quietly in yourself? Be as honest as you like, including if you find this chapter hard to believe or hard to apply.

The turning point is small: the king "looked up to heaven, and my sanity was restored to me" (v. 34). What do you make of the fact that his healing begins with looking up? What might looking up look like for you this week?
4.life: This week, each evening name one thing from your day that you did not earn or control, such as a meal, a kind word, or good health. Say thank you to God for it. Then do one small act of mercy for someone with less power or influence than you.
4.prayer: Thank God that his kingdom lasts from generation to generation and that he is patient with proud people. Ask him to show each person one area where they trust themselves too much, and to give them the humility to look up.
4.tip: People will likely ask whether this really happened, since there is no outside record of the king's illness. Say in one line that Christians differ on whether it records an actual episode or is a story told to make a point about pride and power, then steer back to what the king learned. Also take care with verse 33. It is not a model for how to view people living with mental illness, so keep the focus on pride and humility, not on the king's condition.

5.open: What is something you were warned about ahead of time but had to learn the hard way?
questions: Belshazzar had guests drink from cups taken from the temple while they praised gods of "gold and silver, bronze and iron, wood and stone" (v. 4). Why might he have wanted to do that, and what does it show about his heart?
When the hand appeared, the king's "face grew pale" and his "knees knocked together" (vv. 5-6). Why do you think a man with so much power was so frightened so fast?
His wise men "could not read the inscription or interpret it" (v. 8). Where do people today turn for answers when they are scared, and how well does it work?
Daniel says, "You may keep your gifts for yourself" (v. 17). What does it tell you about Daniel that he refuses the reward before he speaks?

Daniel reminds the king of Nebuchadnezzar and says, "you his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this" (v. 22). Why is it so hard to learn from other people's mistakes?

Daniel says God "holds in His hand your very breath and all your ways" (v. 23). How does it feel to hear that: comforting, unsettling, or something else? Be as honest as you like, including if it is hard to believe.
Verse 27 says, "you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient." How is that different from the grace we read about elsewhere in the Bible, and how might the two fit together?
The king is killed "that very night" (v. 30). What does this chapter say to people who feel that proud and powerful people always get away with it?
5.life: This week, pick one area where you tend to rely on your own strength, skill or reputation. Each day, stop for a moment and tell God plainly that your breath and your days are in his hand, and ask him to help you hold that area more loosely.
5.prayer: Ask God for a humble heart that learns from the past, and thank him that he is the one who holds every life and every kingdom. Pray for anyone in the group who feels powerless or afraid.
5.tip: Verse 27 can sound harsh, and someone may worry that God is always weighing them and finding them lacking. Keep the focus on Belshazzar, who knew the warning and mocked God anyway, and gently remind the group that this is a verdict on proud defiance. Also note that Christians read the chapter's origins differently, and that does not change its warning about arrogance.

6.open: Is there a daily habit or routine you would find hard to give up, even for a month?
questions: The officials looked hard for a fault in Daniel but found "no charge or corruption, because he was trustworthy" (v. 4). What does it look like to be trustworthy in your own work, school or home?
The officials flatter the king into signing a law that serves their own plan (vv. 6-9). Where do you see flattery or group pressure pushing people toward bad choices today?
Daniel "got down on his knees, prayed, and gave thanks to his God, just as he had done before" (v. 10). Why do you think he kept his routine the same, neither hiding nor making a show of it?

King Darius was "deeply distressed" and "labored until sundown to rescue him," yet he could not undo his own decree (vv. 14-15). Have you ever been stuck in a trap of your own making? What was that like?

Daniel says God "sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions" (v. 22). Many of us know faithful people who were not rescued from their trouble. How do you hold that alongside this story? If you have doubts or feel unsure, you are welcome to say so.

Verse 24 says the accusers were thrown to the lions along with their wives and children. Many readers find this deeply troubling. What questions does it raise for you, and how do you want to talk about it?
Darius ends by saying God "is the living God, and He endures forever" (v. 26). Why might it matter to remember that human rulers and laws pass away?
Daniel faced a trap that was not about his work but about his faith. What small, everyday ways do you face pressure to set your faith aside, and what might help you stay steady?
6.life: Choose one regular time this week to pray, even for a few minutes, and keep it the same each day. Notice what it is like to make room for God on purpose.
6.prayer: Thank God that he is the living God whose kingdom will never end. Ask for steady faithfulness in ordinary days, and pray for anyone who is under pressure for their faith.
6.tip: Verse 24 will trouble some people, and others may want to explain it away quickly. Let the group say it is hard, and note that Christians also differ on whether the chapter records events as they happened or is a story shaped later to encourage faithful Jews. You do not need to settle it in one meeting.

7.open: What is a dream you have had that stuck with you long after you woke up, strange or good?
questions: Daniel sees "four great beasts came up out of the sea, each one different from the others" (v. 3). The angel later says they are "four kings who will arise from the earth" (v. 17). Why might the Bible picture human powers as beasts?

The fourth beast is "terrifying, dreadful and extremely strong" (v. 7), and the little horn speaks "words of arrogance" (v. 8). When you look at the powers of our own time, what feels most frightening or out of control to you?

In verse 9 "the Ancient of Days took His seat," and "the books were opened" (v. 10). What does this picture of God as a judge on a throne say to you, and does it feel comforting, uncomfortable, or both?

In verse 13 Daniel sees "One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven." Christians read this as Jesus, Jewish tradition has often read it as the Messiah, and some scholars see a symbol of God's people. What do you notice about how this figure is different from the beasts?
Verse 14 says his "dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away." What difference could it make to believe that no empire, leader or movement lasts forever?

Daniel says he was "grieved in my spirit" and "my face turned pale," and he "kept the matter to myself" (vv. 15, 28). Even after a vision of God winning, he is shaken. When have you found big promises hard to feel, and what would you say honestly about that tonight?

The horn wages war against "the saints" and prevails for a time (v. 21), but in the end the kingdom is given to "the saints of the Most High" (v. 18). How might this help people who feel small, worn down or on the losing side right now?

Christians differ on whether this vision is mainly about a Greek king in the 160s BC, or about Rome and a final enemy still to come. Whichever view you lean toward, what do you think the vision wanted its first readers to hold onto?
7.life: This week, when the news or something in your own life leaves you anxious about who is in control, stop and read Daniel 7:13-14 slowly. Then tell God one specific thing you are worried about, and ask him to help you trust that his kingdom will last.
7.prayer: Thank God that he is the Ancient of Days who sits as judge and that his kingdom "will never be destroyed" (v. 14). Ask him to steady anyone in the group who feels afraid, tired or unsure, and to give them hope.
7.tip: The beasts and horns can pull the group into a debate over who each one represents. Say early that faithful Christians read them differently, name the main views briefly, then steer back to what everyone can share: God judges, a kingdom is given that never ends, and his people are not forgotten.

8.open: Think of a time you were told to wait for something and had no idea how long it would take. How did you handle it?
questions: Daniel sees a ram that "did as he pleased and became great" (v. 4), and then a goat that knocks it down (v. 7). What does it feel like to watch a power that seems unstoppable get replaced by another?
Gabriel names the ram as Media and Persia and the goat as Greece (vv. 20, 21). Why might it matter that God told Daniel the names of these kingdoms before they rose to power?
The goat becomes great, but "at the height of his power, his large horn was broken off" (v. 8). What does that say about how long human power lasts?
The small horn "flung truth to the ground and prospered in whatever it did" (v. 12). Why do you think God's people had to live through a time like that? Where do you see truth getting trampled today?
A holy one asks, "How long" (v. 13). Have you ever asked God that question, and what was behind it? If you would rather not share, tell us what a question like that feels like to hear in Scripture.
Daniel "was terrified and fell facedown" when Gabriel came near (v. 17), and then Gabriel "helped me to my feet" (v. 18). What do you notice about how God's messenger treats a frightened man?
Of the cruel king, Gabriel says, "he will be broken off, but not by human hands" (v. 25). How does that promise land for people who have lived under harsh rulers or unfair treatment?
At the end Daniel admits, "it was beyond understanding" (v. 27), yet he "went about the king's business." What do you do with parts of faith or Scripture you cannot make sense of?
8.life: Pick one thing this week that you cannot understand or fix, and tell God honestly that you do not get it but you are still here. Then get on with your ordinary work, as Daniel did, and tell one person how it went.
8.prayer: Thank God that he sees every oppressor and every season of waiting, and that evil does not get the last word. Ask for patience and steady faith where the answers are not clear yet, and pray for anyone who is suffering unfairly.
8.tip: Verses 9 to 14 and 23 to 25 can pull the group into debates about dates and end-time charts. Say plainly that Christians differ on whether this was fully fulfilled in Antiochus IV or also points to a final enemy, then steer back to what everyone can share: God knows the future, sets limits on evil, and cares for his people.

9.open: When did you last have to say sorry and really mean it? What made it easier or harder?
questions: Daniel reads Jeremiah's promise and then "turned my attention to the Lord God" with fasting and prayer (vv. 2-3). What does it tell us that he responds to God's promise by praying, not just by waiting?

Daniel says "we have sinned and done wrong," even though he is the one person in the book we hear no fault about (v. 5). Why might he include himself? When have you found it hard to say "we" and not "they"?

Daniel says the disaster came as written in the Law of Moses, and that "the LORD our God is righteous in all He does" (v. 14). What do you make of a prayer that says God was fair, and still asks for mercy?
In verse 9 Daniel says, "To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness, even though we have rebelled against Him." Where do you find it easy or hard to believe that about God?

Daniel says, "we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion" (v. 18). How does that change the way you come to God when you have messed up?
Gabriel says an answer went out "at the beginning of your petitions" (v. 23). If you are honest, do your prayers ever feel unheard? What would you say to God about that, or to the group?
Gabriel calls Daniel "highly precious" (v. 23). Why might it matter that this comes in the middle of a prayer of confession? How does it shape how you think God sees you when you repent?
Verses 24 to 27 are hard, and Christians read them in different ways. What do you take from the passage even if the details stay unclear, such as the promise to "make atonement for iniquity" (v. 24)?
9.life: Daniel prayed honestly, naming wrongs and asking for mercy. This week, set aside ten minutes to pray the way he did: say plainly where you or your community have fallen short, then ask God for mercy on the basis of his compassion, not your record.
9.prayer: Thank God that he is a God of "compassion and forgiveness." Ask him to help each of you be honest about where you have gone wrong, and to trust his mercy more than your own record.
9.tip: Verses 24 to 27 can swallow the whole evening. Say at the start that Christians disagree: some see the timeline pointing to Jesus and Jerusalem's fall in AD 70, some to a final period still ahead, and some mainly to the crisis under Antiochus IV in the second century BC. Then guide the group back to Daniel's prayer, which is clear and which everyone can learn from.

10.open: When you are waiting on something important, like news, a package or a phone call, how do you usually handle the wait?
questions: Daniel spent three weeks "mourning" and gave up rich food, meat and wine (vv. 2-3). The text does not say exactly why. What do you think weighed on him, and what do you do when something heavy sits on your heart?
The figure Daniel sees has a face "like the brilliance of lightning" and eyes "like flaming torches" (v. 6). Why do you think Daniel lost all his strength at the sight?
Daniel's friends saw nothing, yet "a great terror fell upon them" (v. 7). Have you ever sensed something bigger than you could explain? How did you respond?
Twice the messenger calls Daniel "highly precious" (vv. 11, 19). What is it like to hear that God sees you that way, and where is it hard to believe?

The messenger says, "from the first day that you purposed to understand and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard" (v. 12). When you have prayed and heard nothing back, what do you tend to assume about the silence? Be as honest as you like, including doubts.

The delay was caused by the "prince of Persia," until Michael came to help (v. 13). Most readers see this as a hint of unseen spiritual struggle behind world events. How does that idea sit with you, and does it comfort you, unsettle you, or leave you unsure?
It takes several touches before Daniel can speak and stand (vv. 10, 16, 18). What does that tell us about how God treats someone who is overwhelmed and worn out?
The messenger tells Daniel, "Do not be afraid" and "Be strong now" (v. 19). Who has spoken strength into your life, and who might need that from you this week?
10.life: Think of one prayer you are still waiting on. This week, set aside a few quiet minutes each day to bring it to God again, and tell him honestly how the waiting feels. Then reach out to one person who is worn out and offer them encouragement.
10.prayer: Thank God that he hears us from the first day we ask. Ask for patience in the waiting, strength for anyone in the group who feels worn out, and trust that he is at work where we cannot see.
10.tip: Verses 13 and 20 about the "prince of Persia" can pull the group into speculation about angels and demons. Briefly say that Christians understand it in different ways, then steer back to what is clear: Daniel's prayer was heard right away, God sent help, and God strengthened him. Also note that Christians differ on who the man in linen is, some seeing a high angel and others seeing Christ before his birth, and leave it there.

11.open: Think of a time you stuck with something when it would have been easier to quit or go along with the crowd. What kept you going?
questions: Most of this chapter is a long list of kings, wars and treaties. Why do you think the Bible includes this much political history, and how did you feel reading it?
Verse 27 says the two kings "will speak lies at the same table, but to no avail, for still the end will come at the appointed time." What does that suggest about who is really in charge of history?
In verse 21 a "despicable person" rises by scheming, and in verse 23 he "will act deceitfully." Where do you see power gained by cheating or flattery today, and how does it affect ordinary people?
Verse 31 describes the temple being desecrated and the daily sacrifice abolished. What do you think it was like for a faithful Jewish family to live through that?

Verse 32 says, "With flattery he will corrupt those who violate the covenant, but the people who know their God will firmly resist him." Why might flattery pull people away from their faith more easily than force does?
Verse 35 says some of the wise will fall "so that they may be refined, purified, and made spotless." Some find that comforting and others find it hard to hear. How does it land with you?
Verse 34 speaks of "a little help" when the faithful fall, and verse 45 ends with a ruler who has "no one to help him." Where have you received help, even a little, when you were struggling?
If you are honest, where does your own faith feel pressured, tired or unsure right now? What would you want God or this group to know about that?
11.life: Pick one small, quiet way this week to stay true to what you believe when it would be easier to go along, such as speaking up kindly, declining something, or keeping a daily habit of prayer. Afterwards, tell one person in the group how it went.
11.prayer: Thank God that he knows the people who "know their God" and holds history in his hands. Ask for steady courage for anyone in the group who feels pressure, and for honesty about our doubts.
11.tip: The chapter is dense with names and wars, and Christians disagree about when it was written and whether verses 36 to 45 describe Antiochus or also a final enemy. Say that plainly in one line, then steer the group back to verses 32 to 35 and the question of what faithfulness looks like under pressure. Nobody needs to follow every king to benefit from the chapter.

12.open: What is something you waited a long time for, and was it worth it?
questions: Verse 1 says "a time of distress, the likes of which will not have occurred from the beginning of nations." Why do you think Scripture is so honest that hard times come before rescue?
In verse 1, God's people are delivered, "everyone whose name is found written in the book." What does it mean to you that God keeps a record of his people?
Verse 2 says "many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake." What hope does this give to people who have lost someone, and what questions does it raise for you?
Verse 3 says those who "lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever." Who has helped lead you toward God, and how did they do it?
Daniel says, "I heard, but I did not understand" (v. 8). When have you read or heard something from God and still not understood it? What did you do?
The messenger says, "Many will be purified, made spotless, and refined" (v. 10). How have hard seasons shaped people you know, for better or for worse?
Christians read the numbers in verses 11 and 12 in different ways. Some tie them to the 160s BC, and some to the end of history. What do you do when a passage stays puzzling?

God tells Daniel, "You will rest, and then you will arise to your inheritance" (v. 13). Daniel gets a promise, not a full explanation. How do you live with questions that may never be answered, and what helps you keep going?
12.life: Pick one question you carry that has no answer yet. This week, tell God honestly that you do not understand, then do one small faithful thing, like encouraging someone or showing up for someone, while you wait.
12.prayer: Thank God that he knows his people by name and that the end of the story is rescue, not ruin. Ask for patience to keep going when you do not have all the answers, and pray for anyone in the group who is waiting or grieving.
12.tip: The numbers in verses 11 and 12 can swallow the whole evening, and Christians genuinely disagree about them. Say that plainly, spend a few minutes at most, and steer the group back to the main promises: rescue, resurrection and a faithful God who tells Daniel to keep going.
